claims.claim: Let D(m,n) be the maximum push number of a sortable m×n instance, N=mn, s=min{m,n}, and t=max{m,n}. Then D(m,n)=O(N·min{s,log t}).
claims.evidence: Assume 2≤m≤n and transpose to a p×q board with p=n and q=m, using transposed target coordinates. The FillColumns proof does not require p≤q: each column is pushed at most p−1 times, and if f columns are underfull, any completed block of q buffer-row pushes either inserts the relevant target-column tokens or makes their columns near-full, decreasing the wrong-body potential by at least f/2. The potential is below (p−1)q/2^(i−1) in each dyadic phase, so each phase costs O(pq), for O(pq log q) total; FloatMinimums costs O(pq). Body-full transposed columns give exactly the hypothesis of claim 6, whose verified construction completes the board in O(mN). Hence D=O(mN). Combining this with the source’s O(N log n) algorithm gives O(N min{m,log n}); transposition symmetry gives the stated bound. One-dimensional cases are O(N).
claims.search_method: Direct dimension-independent re-derivation of the FillColumns potential argument, transpose-state interpretation, and completion lemma; supplemented by exact checks of the completion’s local identities.

claims.claim: For every fixed s≥2, boards with min{m,n}=s have asymptotically tight push number D(m,n)=Θ(mn).
claims.evidence: Claim 0 gives D=O(smn)=O(mn) for fixed s. Translating the sorted s×t board by floor(t/2) columns and floor(s/2) rows has exact distance s floor(t/2)+t floor(s/2), which is at least t floor(s/2)=(floor(s/2)/s)mn. For every fixed s≥2 this is Ω(mn), proving the matching Θ(mn) bound.
claims.witness: The family obtained by translating the sorted s×t board by floor(t/2) columns and floor(s/2) rows.
claims.search_method: Combined the verified upper bound with the independently proved exact translation distance; checked all translations on 2×2 and 2×3 boards by exhaustive BFS.

claims.claim: Every instance A has the displacement certificate pn(A)≥ceil(H(A)/n)+ceil(V(A)/m). Moreover, a global translation by a columns and b rows has exact push number m·d_n(a)+n·d_m(b), where d_k(z)=min(z mod k,k−(z mod k)).
claims.evidence: A row push moves n tokens one horizontal edge, so it can reduce H by at most n, and column pushes do not change H. Thus every sorting sequence has at least ceil(H/n) row pushes. Symmetrically it has at least ceil(V/m) column pushes, and these disjoint move counts add. For a global translation, H=mn·d_n(a) and V=mn·d_m(b), yielding the stated lower bound. Reversing the translation by pushing every row d_n(a) times and every column d_m(b) times attains it exactly.
claims.witness: For the translated board, the attaining word reverses the horizontal translation on each of the m rows and the vertical translation on each of the n columns, always in a shortest cyclic direction.
claims.search_method: Per-push Lipschitz proof for H and V, constructive matching upper bound, and exhaustive exact verification over every reachable 2×2 and 2×3 configuration.

claims.claim: For m,n≥2, a sharper general counting lower bound is D(m,n)≥ceil(log_{d−1}(1+(d−2)(Q−1)/d)), where d=2(m+n), Q=(mn)! if m or n is even, and Q=(mn)!/2 otherwise.
claims.evidence: The parity characterization gives exactly Q sortable configurations. With the d nominal directed push labels, a geodesic contains no adjacent generator-inverse pair, so the number of words of length at most L is at most 1+d((d−1)^L−1)/(d−2). Generator coincidences on length-two lines only make this an overcount. Since a radius-D ball must contain all Q configurations, rearrangement gives (d−1)^D≥1+(d−2)(Q−1)/d; integrality of D gives the claimed ceiling.
claims.search_method: Independent Cayley-ball word count, including direction-label coincidences; exact integer evaluation against exhaustive 2×2 and 2×3 diameters without logarithmic floating point.

claims.claim: Global translations are not generally diametral: D(2,3)=7, whereas every translated 2×3 board has distance at most 5.
claims.evidence: Exact BFS with the seven distinct 2×3 generators reached all 720 states with level sizes [1,7,31,115,274,253,36,3], hence diameter 7. The stated reversed-row configuration has distance 7 and the supplied seven-push word reaches it. Exhausting all six global translations gives distances 0,2,2,3,5,5, so their maximum is 5.
claims.witness: Configuration ((3,2,1),(6,5,4)); an identity-to-witness word is R1-left, C1, R1-left, C1, C3, R1-right, C1.
claims.search_method: Full exact tuple-state breadth-first search of the 2×3 Cayley graph, followed by exhaustive enumeration of all global translations.

claims.claim: On an a×b board with a,b≥2, every even permutation of the positions of one specified row can be performed in O(ab) unit pushes while fixing every other position; the analogous statement holds for a specified column. If a or b is even, every permutation of a specified row or column can be performed this way.
claims.evidence: An even line permutation factors into two involutions with equal transposition count k≤b/2. The positional SwapPairs construction applies them using the same k auxiliary columns and opposite body-shift directions, so every off-row effect cancels; its cost is O(ka+b)=O(ab). Transposition proves the column version, and cyclic relabeling handles any specified line. If the line length is even, one unit line rotation is odd and reduces an arbitrary odd permutation to the even case. If the row length b is odd but a is even, factor an odd permutation as two equal-size involutions and one transposition. The transposition’s only side effect is a cycle on a−1 off-row positions of one column; because a−1 is odd, that cycle is even and its inverse is realizable by the already-proved even column construction in O(ab). The symmetric argument covers columns.
claims.search_method: Re-derived the positional action and cost of SwapPairs, the equal-transposition involution factorization, both parity-repair cases, and the transpose/cyclic-symmetry reductions.

claims.claim: Let 2≤m≤n and N=mn. If every token whose target column is not 1 lies in its target row and the m target-column-1 tokens occupy column 1, then every sortable such board can be sorted in O(mN) pushes.
claims.evidence: When either dimension is even, claim 5 exactly corrects the buffer column and then each of the m rows in O(N) pushes apiece. For odd×odd boards, let β be the buffer-column correction and π_i the subsequent row corrections. Sortability implies sign(β)·∏sign(π_i)=+1. If β is even, perform it and all even row corrections exactly; factor the same adjacent transposition P_i from each odd π_i. The odd rows occur in pairs. On adjacent rows, P_iP_{i+1} is the product of two exact L-shaped 3-cycles, each a four-push row-column commutator; chaining adjacent-row gadgets realizes P_rP_s in O(m). All pairings cost O(m²)≤O(N). If β is odd, choose an odd π_r, factor β into an even column permutation followed by an adjacent vertical transposition P through row r, and factor a sharing horizontal transposition T from π_r. PT is one four-push L-cycle, after which the remaining row-r correction is even; all other odd corrections pair as above. The total is O(mN).
claims.search_method: Complete parity case split and permutation-product audit; exact verification of the four-push L-cycles, adjacent double-transposition identity on 1,225 rectangles, and exhaustive enumeration of all 48 structured 3×3 states.

target_evidence: The exact target asks to close the Θ(log max{m,n}) gap by proving asymptotically tight bounds for the general problem. The draft proves a genuine stronger upper bound O(N·min{s,log t}) and a tight Θ(N) classification for every fixed width s, but for balanced and other regimes with s≥log t it still has only a general Ω(N) lower bound versus O(N log t). Thus it does not resolve the entire target, but it makes material correct progress. The final writeup explicitly calls the result partial and identifies the remaining logarithmic gap, so claimed_resolution=PARTIAL is accurate rather than overstated or understated.
